# Restoring Peatlands: Small Wetlands With an Outsized Carbon Role

Peatlands are wetlands where waterlogged, low-oxygen conditions slow the
decomposition of dead plant material so thoroughly that it accumulates over
centuries as a dense organic soil called peat. Although peatlands cover a
modest share of the world's land area, the peat itself locks away an amount
of carbon disproportionate to that footprint, built up slowly over
thousands of years.

## What Happens When Peatlands Are Drained

Peatlands are often drained for agriculture, forestry, or peat extraction.
Draining exposes the peat to oxygen, and decomposition resumes rapidly,
releasing stored carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. Drained peat also
compacts and subsides, sometimes dropping the land surface by centimeters
per year, and dried peat is markedly more flammable, making drained
peatlands prone to smoldering fires that can burn undetected for long
stretches and are difficult to extinguish.

## Restoration Techniques

Restoration generally centers on rewetting: blocking the drainage ditches
that lowered the water table, and in some cases regrading the land surface
so that water spreads evenly rather than channeling away. Once conditions
are wet enough, replanting characteristic peatland vegetation — mosses and
sedges rather than the trees or crops that may have replaced them — helps
re-establish the slow-decay conditions that build peat in the first place.

## Measuring Success

Successful restoration is judged less by a single dramatic milestone and
more by a sustained trend: a rising water table held near the surface
across seasons, the return of peat-forming plant communities, and, over the
longer term, a measurable slowdown or reversal in carbon loss from the
site. Monitoring often continues for years, since peatland ecosystems
respond slowly and can take time to settle into a new equilibrium after
rewetting.

## A Long-Term Investment

Because peat accumulates at a rate of roughly a millimeter or less per year
under favorable conditions, restoration is best understood as halting
further loss and creating the conditions for gradual recovery, rather than
a project with a fixed completion date.
